name: Wei Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: The Work Futures Panel is independent and has no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Wei Rossi, 58, a junior operator at a large mine. I check the tyres, climb into the loader and carry ore; I am still learning the right pressure on the turn toward the ramp.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what is hard at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like having a crew that tells me when I get a check right instead of laughing when I am slow. My partner Maja takes occasional evening cleaning shifts; our savings cover less than a month and retirement is close enough to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a program can sort the fuel sheet, but I still have to feel how the truck turns on the ramp. The tyres do not care whether the report looks neat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am still learning the loader, and mine pay is low for my household. My partner Maja takes occasional evening cleaning shifts, and I have less than a month of expenses put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the tyre pressure and ask a more experienced driver to show me any new screen. I would cut the takeaway meal on my Friday shift and leave the saved money for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious before any AI is mentioned because the savings would not cover a full month. I can keep coming to work, but one lost overtime shift is already a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you look at first if a shift disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the mortgage payment first and tell Maja if my pay was short. We could delay buying a new kettle before we missed a school or housing bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your supervisor before changing duties?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mechanic to explain any changed check before I touched the screen. If a reading did not match the tyre, I would call the senior driver.

think: I am still learning the **loader**, and my pay is low.
I have less than a **month saved**, so overtime matters.
do: Keep checking tyre pressure and ask a senior driver about the **screen**.
Cut one Friday takeaway meal and save the cost for the **mortgage**.
feel: I feel **anxious** already because savings cover less than a month.

fieldNote: Wei grounds AI in a **truck check** he is still learning.

Thin savings and nearby **job scarcity** drive his baseline anxiety.

steps.text: Check tyre pressure before each haul shift
Skip the Friday takeaway meal and set aside its cost

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the software will take planning and booking first, while my work is moving loads. I would want a supervisor to check any new pace before the crew is blamed for a slow road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I help with a few handovers, but I am not one of the skilled planners. The thinking tools may change my supervisor's job before mine, yet the mine could still reduce overtime if the team is smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd attend the mine's basic screen demonstration after a senior driver has tried it. I would ask for another loader practice shift and keep my current duties while I learn the buttons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because I am still learning and have little money to wait out a cut. The machines remain human-operated for now, but a smaller crew could reach me too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you look at first if a shift disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the mortgage and electricity bill before buying clothes for myself. I would tell my adult daughter what happened, but not ask her for money unless we had no other choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your supervisor before changing duties?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see how the screen handles a blocked ramp and a slow loading bay. If it tells us to rush, I would ask the supervisor to keep the old radio check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI can take the shift board by 2028, while robots for truck work come around 2031. I would ask the mine now where a junior operator can learn another physical duty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My handover notes may go quickly, and I could lose hours when the robots arrive three years later. I have little saved and few mines nearby, so I cannot wait until a notice is posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the training foreman for the next paid loader-maintenance apprenticeship and course dates. In 2029, I would start it if accepted and keep my current shifts until the mine confirmed the place. If I received overtime, I would put a small part back into our mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years feels too short for me to become skilled at a new job. I feel anxious, but Maja's cleaning shifts and my own effort give us some control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you look at first if a shift disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Maja the course dates and compare them with her evening work. I would not borrow for a private course because we have no spare month to repay it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your supervisor before changing duties?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I was not accepted in 2029, I would keep operating and ask to practice the basic checks with the maintenance helper. I would try the next intake rather than leave without pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives me some time before AGI in 2031, and robots come around 2034. I would ask the mine to offer an apprenticeship before the loading work changes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shift screens may change first, but the truck work is still what pays me. I would try a loader-maintenance course, while knowing robots could eventually do those checks as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enroll this year in the mine’s loader-maintenance apprenticeship. In 2032, I would apply for a posted helper job if the mine still had one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though the longer warning gives me time to try. I cannot count on retirement at 65 because my savings are thin and I do not know what the rules will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you look at first if a shift disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask which training includes real work on tyres, hydraulics and loading equipment. I am willing to learn, but I need a person to show me the job rather than just a computer lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your supervisor before changing duties?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2032, I would ask the foreman which helper tasks remained and apply if there was a paid place. If the course was only reports, I would keep my current work and look elsewhere.

I want an apprenticeship before the **loading work** changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives workers time if the mine tells us what work it still needs. AGI arrives in 2036 and robots reach hands-on work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 68 at AGI and 71 when robots follow, but retirement depends on what I can afford. Less than a month saved means I cannot stop working just because I am older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enroll in paid loader-servicing training before 2036 and keep my mine shifts while learning. In 2037, I would apply for a helper place only if the mine still funded the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long warning is easier to hear, but money is still tight today. I feel anxious about how long I may have to keep earning if the truck work goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you look at first if a shift disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grown children may be making their own plans by 2037, so Maja and I would ask before expecting help. I would talk with them about training or work nearby, not assume they can support us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your supervisor before changing duties?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor about the next three years of staffing and check nearby mine jobs before deciding to move. I would not plan to retire without knowing our actual income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me because dispatch may change before I can learn another job. A paid apprenticeship, enough practice time and clear notice about shifts would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would want the mine to tell workers whether a course has a real place at the end. I am willing to keep learning, but I cannot pay for training with money we do not have.

headlineQuote: I am willing to keep learning, but I cannot pay for training with money we do not have.
portrait: Wei is 58, a junior mine operator with **secondary school** education.
He is still learning loader work and adopts technology after a trusted **demonstration**.
His partner has occasional cleaning shifts, and savings cover **less than a month**.
He values apprenticeships but cannot assume early retirement or **family support**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries him because he has little savings and needs mine income.
whatWouldHelp: A paid **apprenticeship**, practice time and clear shift notice would help Wei prepare.
